Encoding the species set

Source: vignettes/articles/encoding.Rmd
encoding.Rmd

A plot’s species list has no fixed length: one plot records three species, the next forty. A neural network reads inputs of a fixed width, so the list has to be turned into numbers first. This step is the species encoding. RESOLVE has five encodings; they differ in how many of a plot’s species they keep, whether two species can end up in the same input, and how much of the representation is learned.

This article covers the five encodings and their settings, the settings that choose which species of a plot enter the encoding, the encoder architectures that read the encoded plot, and a short comparison of the encodings on a small survey.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/resolve/r")

# The RESOLVE engine library, downloaded once
library(resolveR)
resolve.install_backend()
pip install resolve-core

The survey

The examples use the survey of 150 plots in the Alps that ships with the R package, with its 25 species. Preparing the two tables describes the tables and the roles.

plots <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "plots.csv", package = "resolveR"))
species <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "species.csv", package = "resolveR"))

roles <- list(plot_id = "plot_id", species_id = "species",
              abundance = "cover", genus = "genus", family = "family")
targets <- list(elevation = list(task = "regression"),
                habitat = list(task = "classification"))

load_with <- function(config) {
  resolve.dataset.frame(plots, species, roles = roles,
                        targets = targets, config = config)
}
import pandas as pd
import resolve_core as rc

data = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gcol33/resolve/master/r/inst/extdata/"
plots = pd.read_csv(data + "plots.csv")
species = pd.read_csv(data + "species.csv")

roles = rc.RoleMapping()
roles.plot_id = "plot_id"
roles.species_id = "species"
roles.abundance = "cover"
roles.genus = "genus"
roles.family = "family"
targets = [rc.TargetSpec.regression("elevation"),
           rc.TargetSpec.classification("habitat", 0)]


def load_with(**settings):
    config = rc.DatasetConfig()
    for name, value in settings.items():
        setattr(config, name, value)
    return rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets, config)

Choosing the encoding

The encoding is a dataset setting, species_encoding, because the loader writes the tensors the encoding needs. The model takes the encoding from the dataset it is built for, together with the widths that follow from it.

resolve.train.dataset() builds the model from the dataset, so the encoding is set once, in config.

rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset, model_config) copies the encoding, hash_dim, top_k, top_k_species and the taxonomy slots from the dataset into a model configuration. Build every model as rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset, model_config)).

Encoding Model input Learned Species the model never saw
hash a fixed-width vector of hashed species no hashed like any other name
embed the embeddings of the most abundant species, side by side yes the unknown embedding
sparse one column per species in the vocabulary in the first layer no column
rank_pool a weighted sum of species, genus and family embeddings yes the unknown embedding
transformer species tokens, optionally attending to each other, then pooled yes the unknown embedding

An embedding is a learned vector that stands for one species, genus or family. The vocabulary is the list of species the training data holds, with one integer code each; code 0 is reserved for a species outside it. With the genus and family roles set, a species outside the vocabulary still carries its genus and family embeddings.

Hash

The hash encoding maps each species name to one of hash_dim positions and to a sign, and adds the species’ weight there. Two species can share a position; the random sign makes such collisions cancel on average instead of adding up. Nothing about a species is learned, and there is no embedding table, so memory does not grow with the number of species. It is the default encoding, and the only one with a dedicated CUDA kernel for the graphics card.

hashed <- load_with(list(species_encoding = "hash", hash_dim = 64L,
                         selection = "all", normalization = "log1p"))
dim(hashed$hash_embedding())
#> [1] 150  64
hashed = load_with(species_encoding=rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.Hash, hash_dim=64,
                   selection=rc.SelectionMode.All,
                   normalization=rc.NormalizationMode.Log1p)
hashed.hash_embedding.shape
#> torch.Size([150, 64])

top_k (default 3) is the number of species hashed per plot under the default selection = "top", so the default hash encoding reads a plot’s three most abundant species. selection = "all" hashes the whole list. top_k also sets the number of genus and family slots, the fixed positions that hold a plot’s leading genera and families, so raising it widens the taxonomy input too.

normalization rescales the weights before hashing: "raw" (default) uses the abundance as recorded, "norm" divides it by the plot total, and "log1p" takes log(1 + abundance).

Use the hash encoding for a first run on a new dataset, for vocabularies too large for an embedding table, and during a hyperparameter search where the time per run matters.

Embed

The embed encoding ranks a plot’s species by abundance, looks up the embedding of each of the first top_k_species (default 10), and places them side by side. The input width is top_k_species times the embedding width species_embed_dim (default 32). A plot with fewer species fills the remaining slots with the unknown embedding. The slots keep their rank, so the model can treat the most abundant species differently from the fourth.

embedded <- load_with(list(species_encoding = "embed", top_k_species = 5L))
dim(embedded$species_ids())
#> [1] 150   5
embedded = load_with(species_encoding=rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.Embed,
                     top_k_species=5)
embedded.species_ids.shape
#> torch.Size([150, 5])

Every species past rank top_k_species is left out, which is most of a species-rich plot. The genus and family go into top_k fixed slots, filled with the plot’s leading genera and families.

Use the embed encoding when a few dominant species carry the signal, and when you want one vector per species to inspect afterwards.

Sparse

The sparse encoding writes each plot as one row of a community matrix: one column per species in the vocabulary, holding its abundance, or 1 under representation = "presence_absence". Nothing is left out and no two species share a column. The first layer holds one weight vector per species, so its weights can be read species by species.

community <- load_with(list(species_encoding = "sparse"))
dim(community$species_vector_dense())
#> [1] 150  26
community = load_with(species_encoding=rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.Sparse)
community.species_vector.shape
#> torch.Size([150, 26])

The width is the size of the vocabulary, with its reserved slot, so the first layer grows with the number of species and most entries of a row are zero. A species absent from the training vocabulary has no column.

Use the sparse encoding on small to moderate vocabularies, and when the model input should match a community matrix column by column. The heterogeneous graph network below needs it.

Rank pool

The rank-pool encoding keeps every species of a plot. The loader writes, per plot, the species, genus and family codes of each species, a weight and a mask, padded to the longest plot. The model sums each table’s embeddings over the plot’s species, each weighted by pool_weighting.

pool_weighting Weight of a species
"binary" 1 for every species present
"abundance" the recorded abundance
"log1p" (default) log(1 + abundance)
"norm" the abundance divided by the plot total
"rank" 1 / rank, ranked by descending abundance

pool_species_cap bounds the padded width: 0 (default) pads to the longest plot, a positive value keeps that many species, and -x keeps the (100 - x)th percentile of species counts, so -1 cuts at the 99th percentile and reports what it left out.

pooled <- load_with(list(species_encoding = "rank_pool",
                         pool_weighting = "log1p", pool_species_cap = -1L))
dim(pooled$pool_weights())
#> [1] 150   8
pooled = load_with(species_encoding=rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.RankPool,
                   pool_weighting=rc.PoolWeighting.Log1p, pool_species_cap=-1)
pooled.pool_weights.shape
#> torch.Size([150, 8])

Cover dropout (coverDropout in R, cover_dropout in Python, default 0) replaces a training plot’s weights with plain presence at the given probability, each epoch. The model also receives a flag saying whether a plot’s weights carry cover, so a model trained with cover dropout learns to impute plots that come without abundances.

Plot totals (plotTotals in R, plot_totals in Python, default off) add two numbers per plot to the pooled features: the combined cover of all its species, taken as overlapping at random, and the logarithm of one plus its species count. The weighted mean of the rank-pool encoding carries neither, and the attention pooling of the transformer not the count, although both can matter: the EUNIS expert system, for one, assigns most sparsely vegetated habitats only below 30% total cover. With totals dropout (plotTotalsDropout, plot_totals_dropout) a training plot’s totals are withheld at the given probability, and the model learns to impute without them as well; resolve.plot_totals(predictor, FALSE) (R) or predictor.plot_totals = False (Python) then withholds them at imputation, so that an imputed value does not depend on how many species a plot records, as an analysis of species richness may require.

A sum ignores the order of the species, so the encoding holds which species are present and how strongly, and nothing about how they combine. Use it when species richness varies widely, when rare species matter, and when taxonomy is available.

Transformer

The transformer encoding reads the same per-species tensors as rank pooling. It adds each species’ species, genus and family embeddings into one token, a vector of width d_model, passes the tokens through n_attention_layers self-attention layers (default 0), and pools them into one vector. In a self-attention layer each token is updated from the other tokens of the plot, so a species’ contribution can depend on the species it grows with.

Setting (R argument) Default Meaning
d_model (dModel) 128 Token width
n_heads (nHeads) 4 Attention heads per layer
n_attention_layers (nAttentionLayers) 0 Self-attention layers
transformer_ff_dim (transformerFfDim) 256 Width of the feed-forward step in each layer
transformer_pooling (transformerPooling) "attention" How the tokens are pooled
transformer_dropout (transformerDropout) 0.1 Dropout inside the layers

Attention pooling learns a weight for each token and takes the weighted sum. "cls" pooling adds one learned token and reads its output, so it needs at least one attention layer; with none it is refused. With no attention layers the encoding is a rank pool whose weights are learned.

attended <- load_with(list(species_encoding = "transformer"))
fit <- resolve.train.dataset(attended, dModel = 64L, nHeads = 4L,
                             nAttentionLayers = 2L, transformerFfDim = 128L,
                             lr = 3e-4, maxEpochs = 100L, verbose = FALSE)
fit$result$best_epoch
#> [1] 87
attended = load_with(species_encoding=rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.Transformer)
model_config = rc.ModelConfig()
model_config.d_model = 64
model_config.n_heads = 4
model_config.n_attention_layers = 2
model_config.transformer_ff_dim = 128
model = rc.ResolveModel(attended.schema,
                        rc.model_config_for_dataset(attended, model_config))

train_config = rc.TrainConfig()
train_config.lr = 3e-4
train_config.max_epochs = 100
trainer = rc.Trainer(model, train_config)
trainer.prepare_data(attended)
trainer.fit().best_epoch
#> 95

best_epoch is the epoch whose weights the fit kept. The cost of attention grows with the square of the number of species per plot, so pool_species_cap matters more here, and each epoch takes longer than under the other encodings. Attention layers are sensitive to the learning rate and to the reduced range of 16-bit arithmetic: start from a lower learning rate, as above, and leave mixed precision (use_amp, off by default) off when the loss turns into NaN.

Use the transformer encoding when interactions between species plausibly carry signal, on data large enough to fit attention weights, and after a simpler encoding has given a number to compare against.

Which species enter the encoding

Each encoding has a per-plot budget, the number of species it keeps, set by the setting that also fixes its width: top_k for hash, top_k_species for embed, and species_budget for sparse, rank pool and transformer. species_budget defaults to 0, no budget, so those three encode every species a plot records. selection decides which species fill the budget:

selection Species kept per plot
"top" (default) the most abundant
"bottom" the least abundant
"top_bottom" both ends, half each, without duplicates
"all" every species

The embed encoding has a fixed number of ranked slots, so it refuses "all". Its slots follow the ranking: slot 0 holds the most abundant species under "top" and the least abundant under "bottom". A species recorded more than once in a plot, for example once per vegetation layer, enters every encoding once, at its summed abundance.

A budget on a pooled encoding gives a species ablation, a fit that sees only part of each plot. Below, rank pooling reads each plot’s three least abundant species.

rarest <- load_with(list(species_encoding = "rank_pool",
                         selection = "bottom", species_budget = 3L))
dim(rarest$pool_weights())
#> [1] 150   3
rarest = load_with(species_encoding=rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.RankPool,
                   selection=rc.SelectionMode.Bottom, species_budget=3)
rarest.pool_weights.shape
#> torch.Size([150, 3])

representation = "presence_absence" sets every species’ value to 1 in every encoding: the hash and sparse values, the pool weights, the ranking of the genus and family slots and the share of unknown species. The selection still ranks by recorded abundance, so presence-absence under "top" keeps the dominant species.

aggregation ranks the genus and family slots of hash, sparse and embed: "abundance" (default) by the summed abundance of their species, "count" by how many of the plot’s species they hold. Rank pool and transformer carry each species’ own genus and family; under "count" each species counts once in its plot’s genus and family embeddings, instead of at its pool weight.

Encoders above the encoding

The encoder is the network that reads the encoded plot, together with the coordinates and covariates, and produces the plot’s latent representation, the vector every target is imputed from. The default is a multilayer perceptron (MLP), a stack of fully connected layers whose widths hiddenDims / hidden_dims sets. encoder_architecture replaces it with a network from the literature on tabular data, each with its own settings under the name in the table.

encoder_architecture Network
"mlp" (default) Fully connected layers
"ft_transformer" FT-Transformer: one token per input feature, with self-attention across features
"tabnet" TabNet: sequential attention that selects features step by step
"saint" SAINT: attention across features and across rows; at imputation, rows attend to a fixed set of training rows
"excelformer" ExcelFormer: attention guided by learned feature importance
"trait_net" TraitNet: combines the plot’s environment with a trait table per species
"gnn" A graph network over plots, joined by coordinates, taxonomy or composition; trains on all plots at once
"heterogeneous_gnn" A graph network over species, joined by shared genus, shared family and co-occurrence; needs the sparse encoding

Every encoding works with every architecture except where the table names a requirement; a pair that cannot work is refused when the model is built or first run. The graph network over plots joins them by coordinates by default, so it needs the latitude and longitude roles.

fit <- resolve.train.dataset(
  hashed, maxEpochs = 50L, verbose = FALSE,
  modelConfig = list(encoder_architecture = "ft_transformer")
)
round(fit$result$final_metrics$habitat$accuracy, 3)
#> [1] 0.767
model_config = rc.ModelConfig()
model_config.encoder_architecture = rc.EncoderArchitecture.FTTransformer
model = rc.ResolveModel(hashed.schema,
                        rc.model_config_for_dataset(hashed, model_config))
train_config = rc.TrainConfig()
train_config.max_epochs = 50
trainer = rc.Trainer(model, train_config)
trainer.prepare_data(hashed)
round(trainer.fit().final_metrics["habitat"]["accuracy"], 3)
#> 0.867

Training and reading the fit lists the settings of each architecture and the mixture of experts that can sit above any of them.

Comparing the encodings

The loop below fits the survey under each encoding with the default settings and prints the held-out mean absolute error of elevation, in metres. The held-out plots are the share training sets aside and never fits on.

encodings <- c("hash", "embed", "sparse", "rank_pool", "transformer")
mae <- sapply(encodings, function(encoding) {
  fit <- resolve.train.dataset(load_with(list(species_encoding = encoding)),
                               maxEpochs = 100L, verbose = FALSE)
  fit$result$final_metrics$elevation$mae
})
round(mae)
#>        hash       embed      sparse   rank_pool transformer 
#>         261         205         215         177         185
def held_out_mae(encoding):
    dataset = load_with(species_encoding=encoding)
    model = rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema,
                            rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset, rc.ModelConfig()))
    train_config = rc.TrainConfig()
    train_config.max_epochs = 100
    trainer = rc.Trainer(model, train_config)
    trainer.prepare_data(dataset)
    return trainer.fit().final_metrics["elevation"]["mae"]


encodings = ["Hash", "Embed", "Sparse", "RankPool", "Transformer"]
{name: round(held_out_mae(getattr(rc.SpeciesEncodingMode, name)))
 for name in encodings}
#> {'Hash': 222, 'Embed': 173, 'Sparse': 228, 'RankPool': 179, 'Transformer': 152}

These numbers say little about the encodings. The survey has 150 plots and 25 species, the held-out fold is 30 plots, and the starting weights differ from run to run, so the R and the Python run can rank the encodings differently. A comparison on your own data runs each encoding under the same cross-validation folds; Training and reading the fit shows how.

Choosing

Situation Start with
First run on a new dataset hash with hash_dim = 64 and selection = "all"
A vocabulary of tens of thousands of species hash or rank_pool
A small vocabulary, with the input read as a community matrix sparse
A few dominant species carry the signal embed
Richness varies widely, rare species matter rank_pool
Interactions between species matter and the data is large transformer

Settings that travel with the encoding

Setting hash, embed, sparse rank_pool transformer
lr default 1e-3 default 1e-3 lower, 3e-4 as a start
use_amp can be on can be on off when the loss turns into NaN
pool_weighting not read read read
pool_species_cap not read read read, and matters more
selection read, with top_k (hash) or top_k_species (embed); sparse with species_budget read, with species_budget read, with species_budget
species_budget read by sparse only read read
